 Social Security’s Biggest Pay Raise in 4 Years Is Here - But There’s a Catch
 A larger raise is coming, but retirees shouldn't celebrate too quickly.
 By
 Adam Palasciano 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Nov. 3, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google
 Google Preferred Sources lets you customize your search results. By choosing to follow FinanceBuzz, you’re telling Google to prioritize content from a source you trust.
 Social Security recipients have some good news heading into 2027: Their monthly senior benefits are getting a 3.6% boost.
 It's the largest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years, and it could offer welcome breathing room for retirees facing higher everyday expenses.
 But before you start counting that extra money, consider something else. Medicare Part B premiums are expected to rise again in 2027, potentially eating into the increase before it reaches your bank account.
 Here's what the confirmed Social Security raise means for your monthly check and how rising Medicare costs could affect the extra money you receive.

 The 2027 COLA is the largest in 4 years
 The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% COLA for 2027 on October 14, 2026.
 That's the largest annual increase since the 8.7% adjustment that took effect in 2023. For comparison, beneficiaries received a 2.5% increase in 2025 and a 2.8% increase in 2026.
 The COLA is designed to help Social Security benefits keep pace with inflation. It's calculated using changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W).
 The adjustment isn't determined by political decisions or simply by how much prices have increased for retirees specifically. Instead, it follows a formula based on inflation readings during the third quarter of the year.
 The 3.6% increase will apply to Social Security benefits beginning in January 2027. Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients will see their increased payments beginning December 31, 2026.

 Why inflation matters for your Social Security raise
 COLAs are based on inflation , not political decisions. COLAs are intended to help beneficiaries maintain their purchasing power as everyday expenses increase.
 When the cost of groceries, housing, transportation, and other essentials rises, retirees who depend on a fixed income can feel the pressure particularly quickly. That's why inflation readings matter so much when determining the annual adjustment.
 However, there's an important distinction: A larger COLA doesn't necessarily mean retirees are financially better off. In many cases, a bigger adjustment reflects higher prices that have already made everyday life more expensive.
 In other words, the extra money is intended to help you keep up with inflation, not necessarily get ahead of it.
 The average retiree will get roughly $75 more per month
 According to the Social Security Administration's 2027 COLA fact sheet, the average retired worker's monthly benefit will increase from approximately $2,095 to $2,170.
 That's an additional $75 per month, or about $900 over a full year.
 Of course, your actual increase will depend on how much you currently receive. Someone collecting a larger monthly benefit will generally receive a larger dollar increase than someone with a smaller check. You can check your personalized benefit estimate through your my Social Security account.

 Medicare Part B could immediately absorb part of it
Here's where the catch comes in. 
 Many retirees have their Medicare Part B premiums automatically deducted from their Social Security benefits. That means higher Medicare costs can reduce the amount of your COLA that actually shows up in your monthly payment.
 The standard Medicare Part B premium increased from $185 in 2025 to $202.90 in 2026. The final 2027 premium hasn't been announced yet. However, the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report estimates that the standard monthly premium could reach approximately $209.50 in 2027.
 If that projection holds, it would represent another $6.60 per month in Medicare costs. That may not sound like much, but it's money that won't be available for groceries, utilities, or other retirement expenses.
 It's also worth remembering that this is only a projection. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) typically announces the following year's Medicare premiums in November, so the final amount may differ.
 The 2026 COLA experience offers a preview of what could happen
 Retirees have already seen how rising Medicare costs can reduce the benefit of a Social Security raise. In 2026, Social Security benefits increased by 2.8%. For the average retiree, that translated into an increase of about $56 per month.
 At the same time, the standard Medicare Part B premium rose from $185 in 2025 to $202.90 in 2026, an increase of $17.90 per month. That meant retirees enrolled in standard Medicare Part B had to account for a higher premium alongside their larger Social Security checks.
 The same dynamic could play out again in 2027.
 Using the current $209.50 Medicare premium projection, the average retired worker's $75 monthly benefit increase would be reduced by approximately $6.60 after accounting for the projected premium increase. That would leave an estimated $68.40 in additional monthly benefits before accounting for other deductions or changes.
 Keep in mind that this is an illustration based on the projected standard Part B premium, not a guaranteed increase in everyone's take-home benefit.
 Higher earners face another layer of exposure
 Some retirees could see even more of their Social Security increase offset by Medicare costs.
 Higher-income Medicare beneficiaries pay Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amounts, commonly known as IRMAA surcharges . These additional premiums are tied to income levels and can significantly increase Medicare costs for retirees with larger incomes.
 As a result, retirees with higher incomes may pay considerably more for Medicare than the standard premium.
 If you're approaching retirement, it's worth understanding how your income could affect your Medicare costs. Retirement account withdrawals, investment income, and other taxable income sources can all affect whether you owe an IRMAA surcharge.
 Retirement News: Almost 80% of Americans fear a retirement age increase — here’s the real reason why 
 Bottom line
 Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% COLA in 2027, marking the largest annual increase in four years. For the average retired worker, that's approximately $75 more per month, or $900 over the course of a year.
 But don't assume you'll get to keep every dollar of that increase. Medicare Part B premiums are expected to rise again, and higher-income beneficiaries could face additional costs through IRMAA surcharges.
 The projected standard Part B premium of $209.50 would reduce the average retiree's additional monthly benefit by about $6.60 compared with the 2026 premium. The final 2027 premium is still pending.
 Before building that extra money into your retirement budget, consider how much you'll actually receive after Medicare premiums and other deductions. A little planning now can help you eliminate some stress living on Social Security when your new benefit amount takes effect in January.
